$$

after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ u+2v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 2-1\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot x+(-1)\cdot (y-1) \\ (-1)\cdot x+1\cdot (y-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-y+1 \\ y-x-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-y+1,\,v=1y-x+(-1).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+1+(-1)=2.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Matrix Form
content.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 2-1\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-2+1+(-8)=-9.
$$

after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+2v+1 \\ 2u+v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+2v \\ 2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a non-singular matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a parallelogram.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066229/assets/576d60f179b56159504efc59178ada3db798046d01a7dbc92986cd1162f770ea.png)

Consider the affine transformation $T,$ given by

$$
x=u+2v+1,\,y=2u+v-1.
$$

What would be the image of the square shown above under the action of $T?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+2v+1 \\ 2u+v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+2v \\ 2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-3 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a non-singular matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a parallelogram.
